title: Proof Found: A Space Rock Hit the North Sea Long Ago
summary:
About 43 to 46 million years ago, an asteroid crashed into the area where the North Sea is now. It made a giant wave, called a tsunami, more than 100 meters (330 feet) tall. Now scientists say they have proof.

The crash left a hole called the Silverpit Crater. It is hidden about 700 meters under the seafloor, near the coast of England.

Scientists found the crater in 2002. But some thought salt moving underground or volcanoes made it instead.

A team led by Dr. Uisdean Nicholson used sound waves to see under the rock. They also studied rock bits from a nearby oil well.

They found tiny "shocked" crystals. Only a huge crash can make crystals like these. "We were exceptionally lucky to find these," Nicholson said.

Now Silverpit is one of the few proven asteroid craters on Earth.
why_it_matters: Learning about old space rock crashes helps scientists understand how our planet has changed and stay ready for the future.

keywords.explanation: An asteroid is a big space rock that travels around the Sun.
A tsunami is a giant ocean wave.
A crater is a bowl-shaped hole made when something hits the ground hard.
Crystals are solid pieces of minerals with a neat, repeating shape.
Volcanoes are openings in the Earth where hot melted rock comes out.

background_read: Long ago, space rocks sometimes crashed into Earth and left big holes called craters.
Many old craters are hidden under oceans or rock, so scientists need special tools to find and study them.
Only a huge crash can squeeze tiny crystals hard enough to change them, so those crystals are proof of a hit.
